summary:
NASA has decades of Mars data, but it's scattered across dozens of tools built for global views but not the hyper localized areas astronauts will explore on foot. With no GPS, no real-time help from Earth, and communication delays, astronauts must make life-or-death decisions independently, in real time.

Our Solution, MARS (Multi-layer Analysis & Rendering System) is a single, intelligent map that pulls together NASA data such as terrain, hazards, radiation, weather, crew, and science targets into one live, layered view for the astronaut. With multiple features including real-time rerouting, SOS emergency return and weather forecasting,  MARS gives astronauts every answer they need, right when they need it.

Why It Matters? On Mars, the map is the difference between discovery and disaster. MARS (Multi-layer Analysis & Rendering System) makes exploration safer, faster, and possible.
details:
MARS (Multi-layer Analysis & Rendering System) is a navigation and mission support map that acts as a digital companion for astronauts exploring the Martian surface. It pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions topographic, thermal, spectral, atmospheric, radiation, and optical and layers them into one live, hyperlocalized view on the astronaut's visor.

The tool includes multiples core features: Elevation Color for terrain slope, Route for planned paths with waypoints, SOS for emergency return routing, Crew for real-time location tracking, Reroute for instant path recalculation around hazards, Forecast for dust storm prediction, Info for tap-to-reveal data on terrain and minerals, and many more. Every feature is designed around one priority, astronaut safety.

MARS solves the problem of scattered, unusable data by combining everything into one intelligent, glanceable interface. Astronauts can see their terrain, follow safe routes, track crewmates, predict storms, and reveal underground layers all without waiting for guidance from Earth. The tool recalculates routes instantly when hazards appear, warns of approaching dust storms hours in advance, and provides an SOS route back to base with a single tap. The intended impact is safer, faster, and more scientifically productive human exploration of Mars, giving astronauts the confidence to explore further and the data to conduct meaningful science along the way.

If you want to test out the SOS and message function through your Arduino, you may go to our GitHub and check the circuitDiagram.pdf & MARS_SOS_CODE.ino .

MGS MOLA elevation data (Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter, NASA Goddard)
Curiosity REMS weather data (NASA PDS Atmospheres Node)
Curiosity RAD radiation measurements (Hassler et al., NASA NTRS)
projectRefs: ESA Mars Express HRSC camera (part of the HRSC/MOLA blended elevation data)
USGS HRSC and MOLA Blended DEM 200m v2 (source of the elevation grid)
USGS Mars Viking MDIM 2.1 colorized global mosaic 232m (map imagery shown through Mars Trek)
GMT NASA Mars Relief (15 arc-minute grid used to build mars_elev.bin)
Neumann et al. 2003, MOLA global topography of Mars (reference for the elevation data)
Allison and McEwen 2000, Mars clock and season method
jsDelivr (CDN that loads Leaflet and anime.js)
Web Bluetooth API (connects the page to the ESP32 buzzer)
